subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Zeno argued you could never cross a room: first you cover half the distance, then half of what remains, forever. Calculus answers him with one idea — the limit — and everything else in this book is built on it.
learning_objectives: Express the intuitive idea of a limit as the value f(x) approaches, not the value f(x) reaches
Estimate limits from tables of values by approaching the target x-value from both sides
Read limits from graphs, including cases where the function value and the limit disagree
Use correct limit notation, including one-sided notation, to describe function behavior
Recognize the three classic situations where a limit fails to exist

sections.title: Approaching Without Arriving
sections.subtitle: The single most important idea in calculus
sections.body:
A limit answers one precise question: as x gets arbitrarily close to some number a, what single value does f(x) get arbitrarily close to? We write lim x→a f(x) = L, read "the limit of f of x as x approaches a equals L." The crucial subtlety is that x never has to equal a, and f(a) never has to equal L. The limit describes the journey, not the destination.

Think of it like walking toward a wall while filming your distance to it. Even if you stop filming before touching the wall, anyone watching can tell exactly where you were headed. The limit is that destination as inferred from the approach. Whether you actually touch the wall — whether f(a) is even defined — is a completely separate question.

This is why the function f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) is the classic first example. At x = 1 it is undefined: substitution gives 0/0, which is meaningless. But for every x near 1 (and not equal to 1), the algebra simplifies: (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1. So as x slides toward 1, f(x) slides toward 2. The function has a hole at (1, 2), yet lim x→1 f(x) = 2 with complete confidence.

The formal definition (epsilon-delta) makes "arbitrarily close" rigorous, but the AP exam tests the concept, not the formalism: limits describe intended behavior, and that behavior is unaffected by what happens exactly at the point.
key_terms: Limit
The single value L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a from both sides, written lim x→a f(x) = L
0/0 indeterminate form
A substitution result that signals the limit needs more work — it does not mean the limit fails to exist
Removable discontinuity
A hole in the graph: the limit exists but f(a) is undefined or differs from the limit
boxes: ap_alert

The AP exam loves to ask for lim x→a f(x) at a point where the graph shows a hole with a separate filled dot somewhere else. The answer is the y-value of the hole, not the dot. The limit ignores f(a) entirely.

sections.title: Limits from Tables
sections.subtitle: Squeezing in from both sides
sections.body:
Before you have algebraic tools, you can estimate any limit numerically: choose x-values marching toward a from the left (like 1.9, 1.99, 1.999) and from the right (2.1, 2.01, 2.001), and watch what f(x) does. If both columns of outputs funnel toward the same number, that number is your limit estimate.

Tables come with two warnings. First, a table can only ever suggest a limit — it cannot prove one. The function might do something wild between your sample points. The exam phrase "values that best supports" or "estimate" signals that table reasoning is expected. Second, your calculator can lie near the limit point: evaluating sin(x)/x at x = 0.0000001 may suffer rounding errors. Stay close, but not absurdly close.

A table is also the fastest way to detect one-sided disagreement. If f(x) approaches 3 from the left but 5 from the right, the two-sided limit does not exist, and the table makes that visible immediately — two columns funneling to two different targets. This numeric instinct, approach from both sides and compare, is exactly the habit the rest of this unit formalizes.
key_terms: Numerical estimation
Approximating a limit by evaluating f at inputs progressively closer to a from each side
Left-hand approach
Sampling x-values slightly less than a, written x → a⁻
Right-hand approach
Sampling x-values slightly greater than a, written x → a⁺
boxes: ap_alert

On table questions, the AP answer choices often include the value f(a) itself as a trap. Always read the trend of the outputs, not the value at the point — especially when the table sneaks in the row x = a.

sections.title: Limits from Graphs
sections.subtitle: Holes, dots, and jumps
sections.body:
Graphical limit questions test whether you can separate three different objects: the value of the function f(a), the left-hand limit lim x→a⁻ f(x), and the right-hand limit lim x→a⁺ f(x). On a graph, f(a) is wherever the filled dot is. The one-sided limits are where each branch of the curve is heading, regardless of any dots.

Run your finger along the curve from the left toward x = a; the height your finger approaches is the left-hand limit. Do the same from the right. If both fingers land at the same height L, then lim x→a f(x) = L — even if the graph has an open circle there, and even if a filled dot floats somewhere else entirely.

A jump in the graph means the two fingers land at different heights: the one-sided limits exist but disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. A vertical asymptote means a finger climbs without bound — we write lim x→a f(x) = ∞ to describe the behavior, but the limit does not exist as a finite number.

Practice until you can fill in this table for any labeled point on a graph in under ten seconds: f(a), left limit, right limit, two-sided limit. Nearly every graphical limit question on the exam is some permutation of those four cells.
key_terms: f(a)
The actual function value at a — the filled dot on the graph, possibly different from the limit
Jump discontinuity
Both one-sided limits exist but are unequal, so the two-sided limit does not exist
Vertical asymptote
Unbounded behavior near x = a; the limit is described as ∞ or -∞ but does not exist as a number
boxes: ap_alert

When a free-response part asks you to "justify" that a limit exists from a graph, the expected sentence is: the left-hand limit and right-hand limit both equal L, therefore lim x→a f(x) = L. Name both sides — one-sided agreement IS the justification.

sections.title: When Limits Fail
sections.subtitle: The three ways approach can break down
sections.body:
A limit fails to exist at x = a in exactly three classic ways, and the exam expects you to recognize each on sight. First: the jump. The left and right approaches each settle down, but to different values — think of a step function like the greatest integer function at any integer. One-sided limits exist; the two-sided limit does not.

Second: unbounded behavior. Near a vertical asymptote like x = 0 for f(x) = 1/x^2, the outputs grow without any ceiling. Writing lim x→0 1/x^2 = ∞ is a useful description of that behavior, but infinity is not a number, so the limit does not exist in the finite sense.

Third, and most exotic: oscillation. The function sin(1/x) near x = 0 swings between -1 and 1 infinitely often in every neighborhood of 0, never settling toward any single value. No table, no graph zoom, no algebra will produce a destination, because there is none.

Keep the logic straight: 0/0 from substitution is NOT one of these three. An indeterminate form means the limit is undecided pending more work — it often turns out to exist, as with (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1). "Indeterminate" means investigate; it never by itself means "does not exist."
key_terms: DNE
Does not exist — the verdict when no single finite value is approached from both sides
Oscillating behavior
Infinitely many swings near the point, as in sin(1/x) at x = 0, so no destination exists
Unbounded
Outputs exceed every bound near the point; described with ∞ but the limit DNE as a finite number
Indeterminate form
A form like 0/0 whose limit cannot be read from substitution alone — requires algebraic resolution
boxes: ap_alert

Multiple choice answers "the limit is ∞" and "the limit does not exist" can BOTH be defensible descriptions of an asymptote — the exam will only offer one of them. If ∞ appears as a choice for unbounded behavior, that is the intended answer.

mcq.question: The graph of g has an open circle at (3, 4) and a filled dot at (3, 7). Both branches of the curve approach the open circle. What is lim x→3 g(x)?
mcq.explanation: The limit follows the branches of the curve, which approach height 4 from both sides. The filled dot at height 7 is g(3), the function value — irrelevant to the limit.

mcq.question: A table shows f(1.9) = 6.21, f(1.99) = 6.02, f(1.999) = 6.002, f(2.001) = 5.998, f(2.01) = 5.98, f(2.1) = 5.79. These values best support which conclusion?
mcq.explanation: Both sides funnel toward 6. A table can support a limit estimate but says nothing certain about f(2) itself — eliminating C, which confuses the limit with the function value.

mcq.question: For f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3), which statement is true?

choices.B: f(3) is undefined and lim x→3 f(x) = 6
choices.C: f(3) is undefined and the limit does not exist

mcq.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0, so f(3) is undefined. Factoring gives (x-3)(x+3)/(x-3) = x + 3 for x ≠ 3, which approaches 6. Indeterminate means investigate, not DNE.

mcq.question: Which function has a limit that fails to exist at x = 0 because of oscillation?
mcq.explanation: sin(1/x) swings between -1 and 1 infinitely often near 0. Choice A is unbounded, B is a jump (left limit -1, right limit 1), and D actually converges to 0 by squeezing — the x factor crushes the oscillation.

mcq.question: If lim x→5⁻ h(x) = 2 and lim x→5⁺ h(x) = 2 but h(5) = -3, then lim x→5 h(x)
mcq.explanation: The two one-sided limits agree at 2, so the two-sided limit is 2. The function value h(5) = -3 creates a removable discontinuity but has no effect on the limit.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2).
(a) Explain why f(2) is undefined.
(b) Complete the reasoning: for x ≠ 2, simplify f(x) algebraically.
(c) Find lim x→2 f(x) and explain why the answer to (a) does not prevent this limit from existing.
rubric: States that substitution produces 0/0 (division by zero), so f(2) is undefined
Factors x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) and cancels to obtain x + 2, valid for x ≠ 2
States lim x→2 f(x) = 4
Explains that the limit depends only on values of f near 2, not at 2
frq.model_answer: (a) Substituting x = 2 gives (4 - 4)/(2 - 2) = 0/0, so f(2) is undefined. (b) For x ≠ 2, f(x) = (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) = x + 2. (c) As x → 2, x + 2 → 4, so the limit is 4. A limit describes behavior near the point, never at it, so the hole at x = 2 is irrelevant.

frq.question:
The graph of g consists of two pieces: for x < 1, the curve approaches the point (1, 3); for x > 1, the curve approaches the point (1, 5). There is a filled dot at (1, 5).
(a) Find lim x→1⁻ g(x) and lim x→1⁺ g(x).
(b) Does lim x→1 g(x) exist? Justify your answer.
(c) What is g(1)?
rubric: States the left-hand limit equals 3 and the right-hand limit equals 5
Concludes the two-sided limit does not exist BECAUSE the one-sided limits are unequal
Identifies g(1) = 5 from the filled dot
Justification explicitly compares the two one-sided limits
frq.model_answer: (a) lim x→1⁻ g(x) = 3 and lim x→1⁺ g(x) = 5. (b) The limit does not exist: a two-sided limit requires both one-sided limits to exist and agree, but 3 ≠ 5 — this is a jump discontinuity. (c) g(1) = 5, the y-value of the filled dot.

frq.question:
A student claims: "Since substituting x = 0 into sin(x)/x gives 0/0, the limit lim x→0 sin(x)/x does not exist."
(a) Identify the error in the student's reasoning.
(b) Using the table sin(0.1)/0.1 ≈ 0.9983, sin(0.01)/0.01 ≈ 0.99998, sin(-0.01)/(-0.01) ≈ 0.99998, what does the limit appear to be?
(c) State what a table of values can and cannot establish about a limit.
rubric: Identifies that 0/0 is an indeterminate form, which means the limit requires further analysis, not that it fails to exist
Reads the table trend correctly: the limit appears to equal 1
Notes values approach 1 from both sides of 0
States a table can support or estimate a limit but cannot prove it
frq.model_answer: (a) The form 0/0 is indeterminate — it signals that more work is needed, not that the limit fails to exist. Many 0/0 limits exist. (b) Outputs from both sides funnel toward 1, so the limit appears to be 1 (this is the famous special limit lim x→0 sin(x)/x = 1). (c) A table can estimate a limit and support a conclusion, but it cannot prove one, since the function could behave differently between sampled points.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Tables and graphs estimate limits. Algebra computes them exactly — and on the AP exam, exact is the only answer that scores. This chapter is your complete toolkit for evaluating limits by hand.
learning_objectives: Apply the limit laws to break complicated limits into simple pieces
Evaluate limits of polynomial and rational functions by direct substitution when valid
Resolve 0/0 indeterminate forms by factoring and canceling common factors
Use conjugate multiplication to evaluate limits involving radicals
Simplify complex fractions to evaluate limits of compound rational expressions

sections.title: The Limit Laws
sections.subtitle: Why substitution works at all
sections.body:
Limits respect arithmetic. If lim x→a f(x) = L and lim x→a g(x) = M, then the limit of the sum is L + M, the limit of the product is L·M, and the limit of the quotient is L/M provided M ≠ 0. Constants slide out front, and powers and roots pass through. These limit laws are the legal foundation for every algebraic shortcut you are about to use.

Stack the laws together and you get the single most useful fact in this unit: for any polynomial p(x), lim x→a p(x) = p(a). Polynomials are built from sums, products, and constants, and each piece behaves perfectly. The same holds for rational functions — ratios of polynomials — at every point where the denominator is not zero.

So the first move on any limit is always substitution. If plugging in x = a produces an ordinary number, you are done; that number is the limit. Substitution only fails in two interesting ways: a nonzero number divided by zero, which signals unbounded behavior and a vertical asymptote, or 0/0, the indeterminate form that the rest of this chapter exists to resolve.

Keep the two failure modes separate. 5/0 is not indeterminate — it tells you the limit is ±∞ or DNE, and you diagnose which by checking signs on each side. 0/0 tells you nothing yet: the limit might be 7, might be 0, might not exist. Indeterminate means the form alone cannot determine the answer.
key_terms: Limit laws
Rules letting limits distribute over sums, differences, products, quotients (nonzero denominator), powers, and roots
Direct substitution
Evaluating lim x→a f(x) as f(a), valid for polynomials, and rational functions where the denominator is nonzero
k/0 form
Nonzero over zero: never indeterminate — it means unbounded behavior (vertical asymptote), not 'do more algebra'
boxes: ap_alert

The exam tests limit laws directly with questions like: given lim f = 3 and lim g = -2, find lim (2f - g)/(fg). Treat the given limits as numbers and compute: (6-(-2))/(3·(-2)) = -4/3. No curve sketching needed — it is pure arithmetic.

sections.title: Factor and Cancel
sections.subtitle: The standard cure for 0/0
sections.body:
When substitution into a rational function gives 0/0, both the numerator and denominator share a root at x = a — which means they share a factor of (x - a). Factor both, cancel the shared factor, and substitute again. The canceled function is identical to the original everywhere except at x = a itself, and since limits never care about the point itself, the limits are equal.

Take lim x→3 (x^2 - 7x + 12)/(x^2 - 9). Substitution gives 0/0. Factor: (x - 3)(x - 4) over (x - 3)(x + 3). Cancel (x - 3) and substitute: (3 - 4)/(3 + 3) = -1/6. Done — exactly, not approximately.

The factoring toolbox you need: greatest common factors, difference of squares a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b), trinomials, sum and difference of cubes a^3 ± b^3 = (a ± b)(a^2 ∓ ab + b^2), and factoring by grouping. BC students also see polynomial division: if you know (x - a) is a factor because substitution gave zero, dividing it out always works even when the factorization is not obvious.

One warning: after canceling, check the new denominator. If substitution still gives 0/0, factor again — some problems hide a double root. If it gives k/0, the original limit is unbounded and you switch to sign analysis instead of celebrating an answer.
key_terms: Common factor
If substitution at x = a gives 0/0 for a rational function, (x - a) divides both numerator and denominator
Difference of squares
a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b), the most common factoring pattern on limit problems
Double root
A repeated factor that survives one cancellation, requiring a second round of factoring
boxes: ap_alert

Show the canceled form in free response work. Writing (x-3)(x-4)/((x-3)(x+3)) = (x-4)/(x+3), x ≠ 3, then substituting, is the justification readers expect. Jumping straight from the original expression to the answer can cost the reasoning point.

sections.title: Conjugates and Complex Fractions
sections.subtitle: When factoring isn't enough
sections.body:
Radicals block ordinary factoring. The fix is the conjugate: multiply numerator and denominator by the same expression with the middle sign flipped, converting roots into perfect squares. For lim x→0 (√(x + 4) - 2)/x, multiply top and bottom by (√(x + 4) + 2). The numerator becomes (x + 4) - 4 = x, the x cancels, and the limit is 1/(√4 + 2) = 1/4.

The pattern works because (A - B)(A + B) = A^2 - B^2 eliminates the square roots from one layer of the expression. Always multiply by conjugate over conjugate — a disguised form of 1 — so the function's values never change. And resist the urge to expand the unconjugated side; leave it factored, because something is about to cancel.

Complex fractions — fractions inside fractions — are the other classic 0/0 disguise. For lim x→2 (1/x - 1/2)/(x - 2), combine the top into a single fraction: (2 - x)/(2x). The expression becomes (2 - x)/(2x(x - 2)) = -1/(2x), and the limit is -1/4. The universal strategy: multiply through by the least common denominator of all the small fractions, then factor and cancel as usual.

Notice the sign flip trick that appeared: (2 - x) = -(x - 2). Recognizing that a - b and b - a are negatives of each other rescues many limits that look stuck after combining fractions.
key_terms: Conjugate
The same two-term expression with the opposite middle sign; multiplying by conjugate/conjugate clears radicals
Complex fraction
A fraction whose numerator or denominator contains fractions; simplify with the least common denominator
Sign flip identity
(a - b) = -(b - a), used to cancel factors that match except for order
boxes: ap_alert

If a limit contains a square root and substitution gives 0/0, the conjugate is virtually always the intended method. The exam rarely mixes techniques in one problem — one clean tool per question is the norm in multiple choice.

sections.title: A Strategy That Always Works
sections.subtitle: The decision tree for any algebraic limit
sections.body:
Every algebraic limit yields to the same decision tree. Step one: substitute. A real number? Done. A nonzero number over zero? Vertical asymptote — analyze signs from each side to report ∞, -∞, or DNE. Zero over zero? Proceed to step two.

Step two: transform. Polynomial pieces — factor and cancel. Radicals — conjugate. Small fractions inside the expression — clear them with a common denominator. Trig expressions — the special limits of Chapter 4. After transforming, return to step one and substitute again.

Piecewise functions add one wrinkle: at a seam where the rule changes, substitute into each piece separately to get the two one-sided limits, then compare. Equal means the limit exists and equals that shared value; unequal means DNE. Everywhere away from the seams, a piecewise function is just whatever single rule applies there.

This flowchart is worth internalizing to the point of boredom because Unit 4 upgrades it: L'Hospital's Rule will give you a calculus-powered alternative for 0/0 forms. But the AP exam deliberately includes limits where algebra is faster and cleaner — the strongest students know both routes and choose per problem.
key_terms: Decision tree
Substitute first; classify the result as a number, k/0, or 0/0; transform and repeat only for 0/0
Sign analysis
For k/0 forms, testing values on each side of x = a to determine whether each one-sided limit is ∞ or -∞
Seam
An x-value where a piecewise function switches rules — the only place one-sided analysis is mandatory
boxes: ap_alert

For limits at a piecewise seam, the exam expects explicit one-sided work: lim x→2⁻ uses the left rule, lim x→2⁺ uses the right rule, then a comparison sentence. Skipping the comparison and just stating the answer loses the justification point on FRQs.

mcq.question: Given lim x→a f(x) = 4 and lim x→a g(x) = -1, what is lim x→a [f(x)]^2/(g(x) + 3)?
mcq.explanation: By the limit laws: (4)^2/(-1 + 3) = 16/2 = 8. Treat the given limits as numbers and compute.

mcq.question: What is lim x→5 (x^2 - 25)/(x^2 - 4x - 5)?
mcq.explanation: Both give 0 at x = 5. Factor: (x-5)(x+5)/((x-5)(x+1)) = (x+5)/(x+1) → 10/6 = 5/3. (C is the unreduced form — the AP always lists the reduced answer.)

mcq.question: What is lim x→0 (√(9 + x) - 3)/x?
mcq.explanation: Multiply by the conjugate: numerator becomes (9 + x) - 9 = x, leaving 1/(√(9+x) + 3) → 1/(3 + 3) = 1/6.

mcq.question: What is lim x→4 (x - 4)/(x^2 - 8x + 16)?
mcq.explanation: The denominator factors as (x - 4)^2. Canceling one factor leaves 1/(x - 4), a k/0 form: the left side goes to -∞ and the right side to +∞, so the limit does not exist.

mcq.question: What is lim x→3 (1/x - 1/3)/(x - 3)?
mcq.explanation: Combine the numerator: (3 - x)/(3x). The expression is (3 - x)/(3x(x - 3)) = -1/(3x) → -1/9. The sign flip (3 - x) = -(x - 3) is the key step.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = (x^2 - 2x - 8)/(x^2 - 16).
(a) Evaluate lim x→4 f(x), showing the algebraic steps that justify your answer.
(b) Evaluate lim x→-4 f(x) or explain why it does not exist as a finite number.
(c) Identify each discontinuity of f as removable or not removable.
rubric: Factors numerator (x-4)(x+2) and denominator (x-4)(x+4), cancels, and finds the limit at 4 equals 6/8 = 3/4
Recognizes x = -4 gives k/0 (nonzero over zero) and concludes unbounded behavior / limit DNE
Classifies x = 4 as removable (limit exists, function undefined)
Classifies x = -4 as not removable (vertical asymptote)
frq.model_answer: (a) f(x) = (x-4)(x+2)/((x-4)(x+4)) = (x+2)/(x+4) for x ≠ 4, so the limit is 6/8 = 3/4. (b) Substituting x = -4 into the reduced form gives -2/0, a nonzero number over zero, so f is unbounded near -4 and the limit does not exist. (c) x = 4 is a removable discontinuity (hole at (4, 3/4)); x = -4 is non-removable — a vertical asymptote.

frq.question:
Let g(x) = (√(x + 7) - 3)/(x - 2).
(a) Explain why direct substitution at x = 2 fails.
(b) Evaluate lim x→2 g(x) using an algebraic method, showing all steps.
(c) A student instead builds a table and reports the limit is 0.1667. Explain why your answer in (b) is preferable on the AP exam.
rubric: States substitution yields 0/0, an indeterminate form
Multiplies by the conjugate (√(x+7) + 3)/(√(x+7) + 3) and simplifies the numerator to x - 2
Cancels and evaluates to 1/6
Explains exact values beat decimal estimates and tables cannot prove a limit
frq.model_answer: (a) Substitution gives (√9 - 3)/0 = 0/0, indeterminate. (b) Multiply by the conjugate: ((x + 7) - 9)/((x - 2)(√(x+7) + 3)) = (x - 2)/((x - 2)(√(x+7) + 3)) = 1/(√(x+7) + 3) → 1/6. (c) The algebra produces the exact value 1/6; a table only estimates (0.1667 is a rounding of 1/6) and cannot establish the limit, so exact algebraic evaluation earns full credit.

frq.question:
The function h is defined piecewise: h(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) for x < 1, and h(x) = ax + 4 for x ≥ 1, where a is a constant.
(a) Find lim x→1⁻ h(x).
(b) Express lim x→1⁺ h(x) in terms of a.
(c) Find the value of a for which lim x→1 h(x) exists, and state the value of that limit.
rubric: Simplifies (x^2-1)/(x-1) to x + 1 and finds the left-hand limit equals 2
Computes the right-hand limit a(1) + 4 = a + 4
Sets 2 = a + 4 and solves a = -2
States the resulting two-sided limit equals 2
frq.model_answer: (a) For x < 1, h(x) = (x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x + 1, so the left-hand limit is 2. (b) The right-hand limit is a + 4. (c) The two-sided limit exists when 2 = a + 4, so a = -2, and then lim x→1 h(x) = 2.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: One-Sided Limits and When Limits Fail
hook: Functions built from pieces — tax brackets, shipping rates, absolute values — change rules mid-domain. At every seam, the only honest question is one-sided: what happens approaching from the left, and from the right?
learning_objectives: Evaluate one-sided limits using correct notation for left-hand and right-hand approach
Analyze piecewise-defined functions at the x-values where their rules change
Rewrite absolute value expressions as piecewise functions to evaluate limits through them
Apply the existence criterion: a two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree
Determine one-sided limits at vertical asymptotes using sign analysis

sections.title: One-Sided Limits, Precisely
sections.subtitle: Half the approach, all the rigor
sections.body:
The notation lim x→a⁻ f(x) restricts attention to x-values less than a: we slide toward a along the number line from the left only. Likewise lim x→a⁺ f(x) approaches from values greater than a. Each one-sided limit is a full-fledged limit in its own right — it can exist, be infinite, or fail by oscillation — it just uses half the neighborhood.

One-sided limits are not exotic; they are the components of every two-sided limit you have computed. When substitution works smoothly, both sides happen to agree and nobody mentions them. They earn their own chapter because three families of functions force the sides apart: piecewise definitions, absolute values, and functions whose domains end (like √x at x = 0, which only has a right-hand limit at all).

Domain edges deserve emphasis. For f(x) = √(x - 2), asking about lim x→2⁻ f(x) is meaningless — there are no function values to the left of 2. By convention, continuity and limits at domain endpoints are judged one-sided. This matters on exam questions about where functions are continuous: √x is continuous on [0, ∞), with right-continuity at 0 doing the work at the edge.
key_terms: x → a⁻
Approach from the left: x takes values less than a only
x → a⁺
Approach from the right: x takes values greater than a only
Domain endpoint
A boundary of the domain where only one one-sided limit is defined, e.g. x = 0 for √x
boxes: ap_alert

Read the superscript sign carefully under time pressure. lim x→3⁻ means x approaches 3 from below — it does NOT mean x approaches -3. Misreading the minus as part of the number is a classic exam-day error.

sections.title: Piecewise Functions at the Seam
sections.subtitle: Where the action is
sections.body:
A piecewise function lists different formulas for different intervals. Away from the boundaries, limits are ordinary: identify which rule governs the neighborhood and use it. All the interesting behavior concentrates at the seams, the x-values where the active formula changes.

At a seam x = c, the procedure is mechanical. The left-hand limit uses the rule for x < c; the right-hand limit uses the rule for x > c. Compute both by substitution (each piece is usually a polynomial or other friendly function). If the two values match, the two-sided limit exists and equals that value. If not, the limit DNE — a jump.

Watch which piece owns the boundary point itself. If h(x) = x^2 for x ≤ 2 and h(x) = 3x - 1 for x > 2, then h(2) = 4 comes from the first rule, while the right-hand limit 3(2) - 1 = 5 comes from the second. The limit from the left is 4, from the right is 5: the limit DNE even though h(2) is perfectly well defined. Function value and limit are separate bookkeeping, always.

The AP's favorite twist puts a parameter in one piece — find k so the limit exists. Set the one-sided limits equal and solve. Two parameters across three pieces yields a small system of equations; the calculus content is just the existence criterion, and the rest is algebra.
key_terms: Piecewise function
A function defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain
Seam
A boundary x-value where the governing formula changes, requiring one-sided analysis
Matching condition
The equation left-hand limit = right-hand limit, solved to make a limit exist at a seam
boxes: ap_alert

Parameter problems ("find k so that the limit exists") are near-guaranteed on the exam. The full solution is three lines: left limit in terms of k, right limit in terms of k, set equal and solve. Practice until it takes 45 seconds.

sections.title: Absolute Value, the Hidden Piecewise
sections.subtitle: One bar, two branches
sections.body:
Every absolute value is a piecewise function in disguise: |u| equals u when u ≥ 0 and -u when u < 0. Limits through absolute values become routine the moment you rewrite the bars as explicit branches — and treacherous if you don't.

The canonical example is lim x→0 |x|/x. For x > 0, |x|/x = x/x = 1. For x < 0, |x|/x = -x/x = -1. Right-hand limit 1, left-hand limit -1: the two-sided limit does not exist. This function (the sign function) is the simplest jump discontinuity in mathematics, and the exam returns to it constantly in disguises like |x - 5|/(x - 5) or (x^2 - 25)/|x - 5|.

The general method: find where the inside expression changes sign, split the problem at that point, and simplify each branch separately. For lim x→3 (x - 3)/|x^2 - 9|: the inside x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3) is negative just left of 3 and positive just right of 3. The right branch gives (x-3)/((x-3)(x+3)) = 1/(x+3) → 1/6; the left branch picks up a minus sign and gives -1/6. Different one-sided limits, so DNE.

When the inside does NOT change sign at the limit point — say lim x→1 |x - 5| — the absolute value is locally just one branch (here 5 - x, since x - 5 < 0 near 1), and the limit is ordinary substitution: 4. Check the sign first; sometimes the bars are decoration.
key_terms: Absolute value definition
|u| = u for u ≥ 0 and |u| = -u for u < 0 — always rewrite before taking limits
Sign function behavior
|x|/x equals +1 for positive x and -1 for negative x, the model jump discontinuity
Sign-change point
The x-value where the expression inside the bars crosses zero — the only place |·| creates a seam
boxes: ap_alert

If a limit involves |expression| and the limit point makes that expression zero, expect one-sided disagreement and check both branches. If the expression is NOT zero there, the bars are harmless — substitute and move on. That one check routes you to the right amount of work.

sections.title: The Existence Criterion and Infinite One-Sided Limits
sections.subtitle: Putting the pieces together
sections.body:
The fundamental theorem of this chapter: lim x→a f(x) = L if and only if lim x→a⁻ f(x) = L AND lim x→a⁺ f(x) = L. Both sides must exist, and they must agree. Every DNE verdict you will ever justify traces back to a violation of one of those clauses.

At vertical asymptotes, one-sided limits become the precision instrument. Consider f(x) = 1/(x - 2). From the right, x - 2 is a tiny positive number, so f(x) → +∞. From the left, x - 2 is tiny and negative, so f(x) → -∞. The one-sided infinite limits describe the asymptote's geometry exactly: the curve rockets up on one side and plunges on the other.

Sign analysis generalizes: to evaluate lim x→a⁺ of a k/0 form, determine the sign of the expression for x slightly greater than a (test a nearby value or track each factor's sign). Positive means +∞, negative means -∞. Note that 1/(x - 2)^2 behaves differently: the square forces positivity on both sides, so both one-sided limits are +∞, and some textbooks write lim x→2 f(x) = ∞ as a two-sided description of that shared unbounded behavior.

This completes the limit-existence picture from Chapter 1. Jump: sides disagree. Unbounded: a side is infinite. Oscillation: a side fails to settle at all. One-sided language is what lets you say precisely which failure occurred — and exam justifications are graded on exactly that precision.
key_terms: Existence criterion
A two-sided limit exists iff both one-sided limits exist and are equal
Infinite one-sided limit
Notation like lim x→a⁺ f(x) = ∞ describing unbounded growth from one side
Sign analysis
Determining +∞ vs -∞ for a k/0 form by checking the expression's sign on the relevant side
boxes: ap_alert
When justifying that a limit does not exist, name the mechanism: "because lim x→2⁻ f(x) = 4 but lim x→2⁺ f(x) = 7" scores; a bare "DNE" often does not. The one-sided values ARE the justification.

mcq.question: Let f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = 6 - x for x ≥ 2. What is lim x→2 f(x)?
mcq.explanation: Left: 2^2 + 1 = 5. Right: 6 - 2 = 4. The one-sided limits disagree (5 ≠ 4), so the two-sided limit does not exist.

mcq.question: What is lim x→7⁻ |x - 7|/(x - 7)?
mcq.explanation: For x < 7, x - 7 < 0, so |x - 7| = -(x - 7) and the ratio is -1 throughout the left neighborhood.

mcq.question: g(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) for x ≠ 2 and g(2) = 7. Which statement is true?

choices.B: lim x→2 g(x) = 4 and g is discontinuous at 2
choices.C: lim x→2 g(x) does not exist

mcq.explanation: Away from 2 the formula simplifies to x + 2, so the limit is 4 from both sides. Since g(2) = 7 ≠ 4, the discontinuity is removable but real.

mcq.question: What is lim x→3⁻ (x + 1)/(x - 3)?
mcq.explanation: Substitution gives 4/0, a k/0 form. Just left of 3, the numerator is near +4 and (x - 3) is small negative, so the quotient is large negative: -∞.

mcq.question: For what value of k does lim x→1 f(x) exist, where f(x) = kx^2 for x < 1 and f(x) = 3x - k for x ≥ 1?
mcq.explanation: Left limit: k(1)^2 = k. Right limit: 3(1) - k = 3 - k. The limit exists when k = 3 - k, so 2k = 3 and k = 3/2.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = (|x - 4|)/(x - 4) · (x + 2).
(a) Simplify f(x) for x > 4 and for x < 4.
(b) Evaluate lim x→4⁺ f(x) and lim x→4⁻ f(x).
(c) Does lim x→4 f(x) exist? Justify using your answers to (b).
rubric: For x > 4: |x-4|/(x-4) = 1 so f(x) = x + 2; for x < 4: the ratio is -1 so f(x) = -(x + 2)
Right-hand limit equals 6
Left-hand limit equals -6
Concludes DNE because the one-sided limits are unequal, with explicit comparison
frq.model_answer: (a) For x > 4, f(x) = x + 2; for x < 4, f(x) = -(x + 2). (b) lim x→4⁺ f(x) = 6; lim x→4⁻ f(x) = -6. (c) No: a two-sided limit requires the one-sided limits to agree, but 6 ≠ -6, so lim x→4 f(x) does not exist.

frq.question:
The function g is defined by g(x) = ax + b for x < -1, g(x) = x^2 for -1 ≤ x ≤ 2, and g(x) = ax - b for x > 2, where a and b are constants.
(a) Write the equation that makes lim x→-1 g(x) exist.
(b) Write the equation that makes lim x→2 g(x) exist.
(c) Solve the system to find a and b.
rubric: Seam at -1: -a + b = 1
Seam at 2: 2a - b = 4
Solves the system correctly: a = 5, b = 6
Work shows one-sided limits computed from the correct pieces at each seam
frq.model_answer: (a) Left limit at -1 is -a + b; right limit is (-1)^2 = 1, so -a + b = 1. (b) Left limit at 2 is 4; right limit is 2a - b, so 2a - b = 4. (c) Adding the equations: a = 5, then b = 6. With a = 5, b = 6 both limits exist.

frq.question:
Let h(x) = (x + 3)/((x - 1)^2) and k(x) = (x + 3)/(x - 1).
(a) Evaluate lim x→1⁻ h(x) and lim x→1⁺ h(x).
(b) Evaluate lim x→1⁻ k(x) and lim x→1⁺ k(x).
(c) For each function, state whether writing "lim x→1 = ∞" is an accurate description, and explain the difference between the two cases.
rubric: Both one-sided limits of h are +∞ (squared denominator forces positive values)
k: left-hand limit is -∞, right-hand limit is +∞
States lim x→1 h(x) = ∞ is an accurate description since both sides agree in unbounded direction
States that for k no two-sided description applies; the limit simply does not exist, with sides differing in sign
frq.model_answer: (a) Near 1, the numerator is near 4 and (x-1)^2 > 0 on both sides, so both one-sided limits are +∞. (b) For k, just left of 1 the denominator is negative, giving -∞; just right, positive, giving +∞. (c) For h, both sides blow up the same way, so lim x→1 h(x) = ∞ is a fair description of the shared behavior (though the limit DNE as a finite number). For k the sides disagree even in direction, so no single description exists — the limit DNE, full stop.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Squeeze Theorem and Special Trig Limits
hook: How do you find the limit of a function you can't simplify, can't factor, and can't even fully compute? You trap it. The Squeeze Theorem wins by making two easier functions do the work — and it unlocks the most famous limit in calculus.
learning_objectives: State the Squeeze Theorem and verify its hypotheses before applying it
Evaluate limits of bounded-oscillation products like x^2 sin(1/x) by constructing the squeeze
Recall and apply the special limit lim x→0 sin(x)/x = 1
Recall and apply the special limit lim x→0 (1 - cos(x))/x = 0
Manipulate variations such as sin(5x)/(2x) or tan(x)/x into the special-limit templates

sections.title: The Squeeze Theorem
sections.subtitle: Trapped on both sides
sections.body:
Suppose g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) for all x near a (except possibly at a itself), and suppose the two outer functions converge to the same value: lim x→a g(x) = lim x→a h(x) = L. Then f has no choice — lim x→a f(x) = L as well. That is the Squeeze Theorem, also called the Sandwich Theorem: the middle function is pinched between two guards walking to the same spot.

The theorem's power is that f itself can be ugly — oscillating, unsimplifiable, defined by a formula you cannot evaluate directly — as long as you can cage it between manageable bounds. The hypotheses matter, and the exam checks them: the inequality must hold in a neighborhood of a, and BOTH outer limits must exist and be equal. Two guards heading to different spots pin down nothing.

Where do the bounds come from? In practice, almost always from the universal inequalities -1 ≤ sin(anything) ≤ 1 and -1 ≤ cos(anything) ≤ 1. Multiply through by a positive quantity to build the cage. The skill being tested is not finding exotic bounds — it is recognizing that a bounded factor times a vanishing factor is a squeeze waiting to happen.
key_terms: Squeeze Theorem
If g ≤ f ≤ h near a and lim g = lim h = L, then lim f = L
Bounded function
A function whose outputs stay within fixed bounds, like sine and cosine within [-1, 1]
Hypothesis check
Verifying the inequality holds near a and that both outer limits agree — required for credit
boxes: ap_alert

When the AP gives you an inequality like 1 - x^2/4 ≤ g(x) ≤ cos(x) and asks for lim x→0 g(x), it is handing you a Squeeze Theorem question. Evaluate both ends (both → 1 here), say they are equal, cite the theorem by name, and conclude. All three sentences are graded.

sections.title: The Classic Squeeze
sections.subtitle: x^2 sin(1/x) and its family
sections.body:
Recall from Chapter 1 that sin(1/x) has no limit at 0 — it oscillates forever. Now multiply it by x^2 and watch the pathology get cured: f(x) = x^2 sin(1/x). However wildly the sine factor swings, it stays in [-1, 1], so -x^2 ≤ x^2 sin(1/x) ≤ x^2 for every x ≠ 0.

Both guards converge: lim x→0 (-x^2) = 0 and lim x→0 x^2 = 0. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim x→0 x^2 sin(1/x) = 0. The vanishing envelope x^2 crushes the oscillation. Graphically, the curve wiggles infinitely fast but inside an ever-narrowing parabolic funnel pinched to a point at the origin.

The construction generalizes: (anything → 0) × (anything bounded) → 0. So x sin(1/x) → 0, x^4 cos(1/x^2) → 0, and √x sin(1/x) → 0 from the right. Contrast with sin(1/x) alone (no vanishing factor — DNE) and with (1/x) sin(x)... which is a different story entirely, headed for the next section.

Write the squeeze explicitly on free-response questions. The chain -|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| (using absolute values when x can be negative — multiplying an inequality by a negative number flips it!) shows the grader you respected the theorem's hypotheses rather than waving at "bounded times zero."
key_terms: Vanishing envelope
A factor like x^2 that tends to 0 and bounds the entire product inside a shrinking funnel
Bounded times vanishing
The product of a bounded function and a function tending to 0 has limit 0 — proved via squeeze
Inequality flip
Multiplying an inequality by a negative quantity reverses it; use |x| envelopes to stay safe
boxes: ap_alert

The justification "sin(1/x) is bounded between -1 and 1, and x^2 → 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the product → 0" is the exact sentence pattern graders look for. Memorize the sentence, not just the answer.

sections.title: The Most Famous Limit in Calculus
sections.subtitle: sin(x)/x → 1
sections.body:
At x = 0, sin(x)/x is a 0/0 form that no amount of factoring will fix — sine is not a polynomial. Yet the limit exists: lim x→0 sin(x)/x = 1 (x in radians). Numerically the evidence is overwhelming: sin(0.1)/0.1 ≈ 0.99833, sin(0.01)/0.01 ≈ 0.9999833. For tiny angles, sin(x) and x are nearly indistinguishable.

The standard proof is itself a Squeeze Theorem showcase. Comparing areas of a triangle, a circular sector, and a larger triangle in the unit circle produces, for 0 < x < π/2, the inequality cos(x) ≤ sin(x)/x ≤ 1. As x → 0⁺, cos(x) → 1, so the ratio is squeezed to 1; symmetry handles the left side. The geometry explains the radian requirement — sector area formulas assume radian measure, which is why calculus lives in radians forever after.

Its companion limit: lim x→0 (1 - cos(x))/x = 0. Multiply by the conjugate (1 + cos(x)) to get sin^2(x)/(x(1 + cos(x))) = (sin(x)/x) · sin(x)/(1 + cos(x)) → 1 · 0/2 = 0. Worth knowing both the result and that two-line derivation — the conjugate trick from Chapter 2 reappearing on trig turf.

These two limits are the seeds of Unit 2: the derivative of sin(x) at 0 IS lim h→0 sin(h)/h, and the derivative formulas for all of trigonometry trace back to these two facts. Learn them as permanent equipment, not chapter trivia.
key_terms: Special limit 1
lim x→0 sin(x)/x = 1, valid in radian measure
Special limit 2
lim x→0 (1 - cos(x))/x = 0, derived from the first via conjugate
Radian requirement
Both special limits and all of calculus's trig derivatives assume angles measured in radians
boxes: ap_alert

Calculator in degree mode silently breaks every trig limit and derivative on the exam — sin(x)/x in degrees approaches π/180, not 1. Radian mode is the first thing to check when your calculator section answers look inexplicably wrong.

sections.title: Stretching the Templates
sections.subtitle: sin(5x)/(2x) and friends
sections.body:
The exam rarely serves sin(x)/x plain. It serves sin(5x)/(2x), tan(3x)/x, sin(x^2)/x, or sin(2x)/sin(7x) — and expects you to bend each into the template lim u→0 sin(u)/u = 1 where u is whatever lives inside the sine.

The mechanical rule: match the inside. For lim x→0 sin(5x)/(2x), force a 5x downstairs: sin(5x)/(2x) = (5/2) · sin(5x)/(5x). As x → 0, 5x → 0 too, so the ratio → 1 and the limit is 5/2. In general lim x→0 sin(ax)/(bx) = a/b. The coefficient migrates out; the template eats the rest.

Tangent variations unpack via tan(u) = sin(u)/cos(u): tan(3x)/x = (sin(3x)/(3x)) · 3 · (1/cos(3x)) → 1 · 3 · 1 = 3. Ratios of sines split into two templates: sin(2x)/sin(7x) = (sin(2x)/(2x)) · (7x/sin(7x)) · (2/7) → 2/7. Every variation is bookkeeping around the same engine.

Two cautions. First, the template needs its inside going to 0: lim x→π sin(x)/x is NOT a special limit — substitute directly to get 0/π = 0. Second, sin(x^2)/x = x · sin(x^2)/x^2 → 0 · 1 = 0: rewrite until each sine sits over its own inside, then read off what is left. If the insides cannot match, you are probably looking at an ordinary substitution problem wearing a trig costume.
key_terms: Template matching
Rewriting so each sin(u) sits over the same u, then applying sin(u)/u → 1
a/b rule
lim x→0 sin(ax)/(bx) = a/b, the workhorse result for linear insides
Inside check
The special limits apply only when the sine's argument tends to 0 — verify before templating
boxes: ap_alert

Fastest exam check: for small angles sin(u) ≈ u, so sin(5x)/(2x) ≈ 5x/2x = 5/2. This approximation instantly predicts every a/b-type answer — use it to verify your algebra, then write the rigorous template steps for the FRQ.

mcq.question: If 4 - x^2 ≤ f(x) ≤ 4 + x^2 for all x near 0, what is lim x→0 f(x)?
mcq.explanation: Both bounding functions approach 4 as x → 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem f is forced to 4 as well.

mcq.question: What is lim x→0 x^4 cos(3/x)?
mcq.explanation: Cosine is bounded: -x^4 ≤ x^4 cos(3/x) ≤ x^4, and both ends go to 0. Bounded times vanishing is 0 by the squeeze.

mcq.question: What is lim x→0 sin(7x)/(3x)?
mcq.explanation: Rewrite as (7/3)·sin(7x)/(7x). The template sin(u)/u → 1 with u = 7x gives 7/3.

mcq.question: What is lim x→0 (1 - cos(x))/(5x)?
mcq.explanation: (1/5)·(1 - cos x)/x → (1/5)·0 = 0, using the second special limit.

mcq.question: What is lim x→π sin(x)/x?
mcq.explanation: The inside does not approach 0, so this is not the special limit. Direct substitution: sin(π)/π = 0/π = 0.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x^2 sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0.
(a) Explain why lim x→0 sin(1/x) does not exist.
(b) Write a chain of inequalities bounding f(x) near 0.
(c) Use the Squeeze Theorem to evaluate lim x→0 f(x), citing each hypothesis of the theorem.
rubric: States sin(1/x) oscillates between -1 and 1 infinitely often near 0, never approaching a single value
Writes -x^2 ≤ x^2 sin(1/x) ≤ x^2 for x ≠ 0
Evaluates both outer limits as 0
Cites the Squeeze Theorem and concludes the limit equals 0
frq.model_answer: (a) As x → 0, 1/x runs through infinitely many periods of sine, so sin(1/x) keeps swinging between -1 and 1 — no single approached value. (b) Since -1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 and x^2 > 0, multiplying gives -x^2 ≤ x^2 sin(1/x) ≤ x^2. (c) lim x→0 (-x^2) = 0 and lim x→0 x^2 = 0; the bounds hold for all x ≠ 0 near 0 and the outer limits agree, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim x→0 x^2 sin(1/x) = 0.

frq.question:
Evaluate each limit, showing the rewriting that justifies your answer.
(a) lim x→0 sin(4x)/sin(9x)
(b) lim x→0 tan(2x)/(5x)
(c) lim x→0 sin(x^3)/x
rubric: (a) Splits into (sin 4x/4x)·(9x/sin 9x)·(4/9) and evaluates to 4/9
(b) Uses tan = sin/cos: (sin 2x/2x)·(2/5)·(1/cos 2x) → 2/5
(c) Writes x^2 · sin(x^3)/x^3 → 0 · 1 = 0
Each special-limit application notes the inside tends to 0
frq.model_answer: (a) sin(4x)/sin(9x) = (sin 4x/4x)·(9x/sin 9x)·(4/9) → 1·1·(4/9) = 4/9. (b) tan(2x)/(5x) = (sin 2x)/(2x) · (2/5) · 1/cos(2x) → 1 · 2/5 · 1 = 2/5. (c) sin(x^3)/x = x^2 · sin(x^3)/x^3; as x → 0 the template factor → 1 and x^2 → 0, so the limit is 0.

frq.question:
Suppose g satisfies 2x + 1 ≤ g(x) ≤ x^2 + 2 for all x in (0, 3).
(a) Evaluate lim x→1 g(x) if possible, and justify.
(b) Explain why the given inequality does NOT determine lim x→2 g(x).
(c) What additional single piece of information would determine lim x→2 g(x)? Give an example.
rubric: (a) Both bounds equal 3 at x = 1 (limits 3 and 3); cites Squeeze Theorem; concludes 3
(b) Notes the bounds at x = 2 are 5 and 6, which differ, so the squeeze fails
(c) Recognizes that tighter bounds agreeing at 2 (or the value of the limit directly) would suffice
Provides a valid example, e.g. a second inequality pinching g between functions that both → 5
frq.model_answer: (a) lim x→1 (2x + 1) = 3 and lim x→1 (x^2 + 2) = 3. The bounds agree, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim x→1 g(x) = 3. (b) At x = 2 the lower bound approaches 5 and the upper bound 6; guards arriving at different places pin nothing down, so the theorem does not apply. (c) Any tighter cage whose sides agree at x = 2 — for example, also knowing g(x) ≤ 2x + 1 + (x-1)(x-2)^2 near 2, or simply tightening to bounds that both approach 5 — would force the limit to that common value.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: You already know continuity when you see it — a curve drawn without lifting your pencil. Calculus upgrades that instinct into a three-part test precise enough to grade, and the AP exam grades it constantly.
learning_objectives: State and apply the three-part definition of continuity at a point
Classify discontinuities as removable, jump, or infinite from formulas and graphs
Determine continuity on intervals, including one-sided continuity at endpoints
Find parameter values that make piecewise functions continuous
Redefine functions to remove removable discontinuities

sections.title: The Three-Part Test
sections.subtitle: What 'no pencil lift' actually means
sections.body:
A function f is continuous at x = a when three things hold, in order: (1) f(a) exists — the point is actually on the graph; (2) lim x→a f(x) exists — both one-sided limits exist and agree; (3) the two are equal: lim x→a f(x) = f(a). The third condition is the punchline: the value the function approaches is the value it delivers.

Each condition can fail independently, and each failure has a name you will assign in a moment. A hole with no dot fails (1). A jump fails (2). A hole with the dot floating elsewhere passes (1) and (2) but fails (3). Train yourself to check the conditions in order and report the first one that breaks — that is exactly the justification format FRQ graders reward.

Most functions you meet are continuous everywhere they are defined: polynomials on all of ℝ; rational functions, roots, trig, exponentials, and logarithms on their domains. Sums, differences, products, quotients (nonzero denominator), and compositions of continuous functions stay continuous. This 'library of continuous functions' is why substitution computes most limits — continuity is the license for substitution.

The definition also explains why limits and continuity are taught together: continuity at a is a statement ABOUT a limit. Write the three conditions once at the top of your scratch paper on exam day; half the unit's questions are one of the three conditions wearing a costume.
key_terms: Continuity at a point
f(a) exists, lim x→a f(x) exists, and the two are equal
Library of continuous functions
Polynomials, rationals, roots, trig, exponentials, logs — continuous on their domains
License for substitution
If f is continuous at a, then lim x→a f(x) = f(a) by definition
boxes: ap_alert

FRQ justifications must cite the definition, not the pencil: 'f is continuous at 2 because lim x→2 f(x) = f(2) = 5' scores the point. 'The graph has no break' does not. Always produce the limit value and the function value and say they match.

sections.title: A Field Guide to Discontinuities
sections.subtitle: Removable, jump, infinite
sections.body:
Removable discontinuity: the limit exists but condition (1) or (3) fails — a hole, with or without a stray dot. The name is literal: redefine the single value f(a) := lim x→a f(x) and continuity is repaired. Algebraically these arise from canceled common factors, like (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1.

Jump discontinuity: both one-sided limits exist but disagree. No single-point repair can fix a jump — the two branches genuinely arrive at different heights. Jumps come from piecewise definitions and absolute-value expressions, the Chapter 3 cast. Note that f(a) may equal either branch or neither; the jump is about the limits, not the dot.

Infinite discontinuity: at least one one-sided limit is ±∞ — a vertical asymptote. Condition (2) fails catastrophically. These come from k/0 forms: denominators vanishing where numerators do not. (A 0/0 point might be a hole OR an asymptote — factor first, then classify by what survives in the denominator.)

One more case rounds out the taxonomy for the curious: oscillating discontinuities like sin(1/x) at 0, where a one-sided limit fails to exist for neither jump nor infinite reasons. The AP tests the main three; recognize oscillation as 'limit DNE, not a jump, not infinite' if it appears.
key_terms: Removable discontinuity
The limit exists but doesn't match f(a) (or f(a) is undefined); fixable by redefining one point
Jump discontinuity
One-sided limits exist but differ; arises at piecewise seams; not fixable by one point
Infinite discontinuity
A vertical asymptote — at least one one-sided limit is ±∞
Classification by factoring
For rational functions: canceled factors give holes, surviving denominator zeros give asymptotes
boxes: ap_alert

For f(x) = (x-3)(x+1)/((x-3)(x-5)): x = 3 is removable (the factor cancels) but x = 5 is infinite (the factor survives). The exam loves rational functions with one of each — classify per point, never per function.

sections.title: Continuity on Intervals
sections.subtitle: Open, closed, and the endpoint convention
sections.body:
Continuity on an open interval (a, b) means continuity at every interior point — nothing new. Closed intervals require the endpoint convention: f is continuous on [a, b] when it is continuous on (a, b), right-continuous at a (lim x→a⁺ f(x) = f(a)), and left-continuous at b. Endpoints are judged one-sided because the other side does not exist in the domain.

This convention is why √x earns the title 'continuous on [0, ∞)': at 0 there is nothing to the left, the right-hand limit is 0, and √0 = 0 — the one-sided check passes. Same logic certifies √(4 - x^2) as continuous on [-2, 2], a semicircle including both endpoints.

When an exam question asks for ALL x-values where a function is discontinuous, work the domain first. A rational function is discontinuous exactly at the zeros of its denominator (classify each as hole or asymptote). A piecewise function adds its seams to the suspect list — check the three-part test at each seam. Everything else is covered by the library of continuous functions.

Interval language matters for the big theorems coming next: the Intermediate Value Theorem and, later, the Extreme Value Theorem demand continuity on a CLOSED interval. Knowing precisely what that requires — including the one-sided endpoint checks — is what lets you verify hypotheses instead of hand-waving them.
key_terms: Continuity on (a, b)
Continuous at every point strictly between a and b
Continuity on [a, b]
Continuous on (a, b), plus right-continuity at a and left-continuity at b
Endpoint convention
Domain edges are checked with one-sided limits only
boxes: ap_alert

When listing discontinuities of a rational function, the AP expects you to check the denominator's zeros and ONLY those. Saying 'discontinuous at x = 2 and 5 because the denominator is zero there' plus a hole/asymptote classification is a complete answer.

sections.title: Engineering Continuity
sections.subtitle: Parameters, repairs, and extensions
sections.body:
The unit's signature FRQ skill: choose constants to make a piecewise function continuous. At each seam, continuity demands left-hand limit = right-hand limit = function value. With one parameter, that is one equation; with two parameters and two seams, a 2×2 system. The calculus is the setup; the algebra is the finish.

Example: f(x) = (x^2 - 16)/(x - 4) for x ≠ 4 and f(4) = c. The limit as x → 4 is 8 (factor and cancel), so continuity needs c = 8 — and with that single choice the removable discontinuity is repaired. This 'continuous extension' idea is exactly why removable discontinuities are called removable.

A twist the exam enjoys: trig pieces. To make f(x) = sin(kx)/x for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 3 continuous at 0, recall the special limit: sin(kx)/x → k. So k = 3. The special limits of Chapter 4 routinely smuggle themselves into continuity problems — recognize the template under the new packaging.

Finally, connect continuity to its consequences. Continuous functions can be evaluated by substitution, are guaranteed intermediate values (next chapter), attain extremes on closed intervals (Unit 5), and are integrable (Unit 6). When a later theorem demands continuity as a hypothesis, this chapter is the checklist you run.
key_terms: Matching condition
At each seam: left limit = right limit = f(seam), the equation(s) that determine parameters
Continuous extension
Redefining f at a removable discontinuity so the repaired function is continuous
Hypothesis checking
Verifying continuity before invoking IVT, EVT, or integrability
boxes: ap_alert

Show all three quantities at a seam — left limit, right limit, function value — even when two are obviously equal. The continuity point on FRQs is awarded for demonstrating the definition, and the fastest way to lose it is silently assuming f(c) equals one of the limits.

mcq.question: Let f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = 5. Which condition of continuity fails at x = 3?

choices.C: The limit exists but does not equal f(3)

mcq.explanation: The limit is 6 (factor and cancel) and f(3) = 5. Conditions (1) and (2) pass; (3) fails since 6 ≠ 5. Removable discontinuity.

mcq.question: g(x) = (x + 2)/((x + 2)(x - 7)). The discontinuities of g are best described as
mcq.explanation: The (x + 2) factor cancels — a hole at x = -2 (limit exists, equals -1/9). The (x - 7) factor survives in the denominator — vertical asymptote at 7.

mcq.question: For what value of c is f continuous at x = 2, where f(x) = cx^2 + 1 for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 4x - c for x > 2?
mcq.explanation: Left value: 4c + 1. Right limit: 8 - c. Continuity: 4c + 1 = 8 - c, so 5c = 7, c = 7/5.

mcq.question: Which function is continuous on the closed interval [0, 4]?
mcq.explanation: C is defined on all of [0, 4] and continuous, with one-sided continuity at both endpoints. A has an asymptote at 2; B is undefined on [0, 1); D has a hole at 2.

mcq.question: To make h(x) = sin(5x)/(2x) for x ≠ 0 continuous at 0, define h(0) =
mcq.explanation: The limit as x → 0 is 5/2 by the special limit template. Continuity requires h(0) to equal the limit.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = (x^2 + x - 12)/(x - 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = k.
(a) Find lim x→3 f(x).
(b) Determine the value of k that makes f continuous at x = 3, citing the definition of continuity.
(c) With your value of k, classify the original discontinuity and explain why the name is appropriate.
rubric: Factors to (x + 4)(x - 3)/(x - 3) and finds the limit equals 7
Sets k = 7 and states all three continuity conditions hold
Identifies the discontinuity (for general k ≠ 7) as removable
Explains 'removable' means repairable by redefining the single value f(3)
frq.model_answer: (a) f(x) = (x + 4)(x - 3)/(x - 3) = x + 4 for x ≠ 3, so the limit is 7. (b) Continuity at 3 requires f(3) to exist, the limit to exist, and the two to be equal; the limit is 7, so k = 7. (c) The discontinuity is removable: the limit exists, and changing only the single value f(3) to 7 removes it — exactly what the name promises.

frq.question:
The function g is defined by g(x) = a x + 3 for x < 1, g(x) = 5 for x = 1, and g(x) = x^2 + b for x > 1.
(a) Write the conditions required for g to be continuous at x = 1.
(b) Solve for a and b.
(c) Suppose instead b is chosen so the right-hand limit is 9. What type of discontinuity results, regardless of a? Explain.
rubric: Conditions: a + 3 = 5 and 1 + b = 5 (both one-sided limits equal g(1) = 5)
Solves a = 2, b = 4
With right limit 9 ≠ g(1) = 5: if a + 3 = 9 the limit exists but ≠ 5 (removable-by-redefinition mismatch); otherwise jump
Explains classification depends on whether one-sided limits agree, and they cannot both equal g(1)
frq.model_answer: (a) Continuity needs lim x→1⁻ g = lim x→1⁺ g = g(1) = 5: that is, a(1) + 3 = 5 and 1^2 + b = 5. (b) a = 2 and b = 4. (c) With 1 + b = 9, the right-hand limit is 9 while g(1) = 5. If a + 3 = 9 too, the two-sided limit is 9 ≠ 5: the discontinuity is removable (redefine g(1) = 9). If a + 3 ≠ 9 the one-sided limits disagree: a jump. Either way g is discontinuous at 1, since both limits can never match the required value 5 simultaneously with the right limit forced to 9.

frq.question:
Consider r(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - 2x - 8).
(a) Find all x-values where r is discontinuous.
(b) Classify each discontinuity, with algebraic justification.
(c) Define a new function R(x) that extends r continuously wherever possible, and state the largest set on which R is continuous.
rubric: Denominator zeros: x = 4 and x = -2
Factors: (x-2)(x+2)/((x-4)(x+2)); x = -2 removable (limit = 0/(-6)... compute: (x-2)/(x-4) at -2 = (-4)/(-6) = 2/3), x = 4 infinite
Defines R(x) = r(x) for x ∉ {-2, 4} and R(-2) = 2/3
States R is continuous on ℝ except x = 4 (vertical asymptote cannot be repaired)
frq.model_answer: (a) The denominator factors as (x - 4)(x + 2), so r is discontinuous at x = 4 and x = -2. (b) Numerator: (x - 2)(x + 2). The (x + 2) cancels, so at x = -2 the limit is (x - 2)/(x - 4) = (-4)/(-6) = 2/3: removable. At x = 4 the reduced denominator still vanishes while the numerator is 2/0 — k/0: infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote). (c) Let R(x) = (x - 2)/(x - 4) with R(-2) = 2/3 — equivalently r extended by that one value. R is continuous on all reals except x = 4, where no single-point definition can repair unbounded behavior.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: If you were five feet tall in sixth grade and six feet tall now, there was a moment you were exactly 5'7". Obvious? The Intermediate Value Theorem is that obviousness weaponized — it proves equations have solutions without ever solving them.
learning_objectives: State the Intermediate Value Theorem with all of its hypotheses
Verify IVT hypotheses explicitly before applying the theorem
Use the IVT to prove an equation has a root in a given interval
Apply the IVT to table-based problems to guarantee specific function values
Identify what the IVT does and does not claim, including its converse's failure

sections.title: What the Theorem Says
sections.subtitle: Continuity means no skipped values
sections.body:
The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT): if f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b], and N is any number strictly between f(a) and f(b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) with f(c) = N. A continuous function cannot get from one height to another without passing through every height in between.

Every word is load-bearing. Continuous on the CLOSED interval — a single discontinuity gives the function a trapdoor to skip values. Between f(a) and f(b) — the theorem promises nothing about values outside that bracket (though the function may hit them anyway). At least one c — there may be many crossings; IVT guarantees existence, never uniqueness. In (a, b) — the c is strictly inside.

The theorem is an existence statement, and that is precisely its power and its limitation: it tells you a value is achieved but gives zero information about where. Finding c is your algebra's job; certifying that c exists is the IVT's job. On the AP, the certification IS the answer — many IVT questions never ask for c at all.

Intuition check: why does continuity matter? Picture f(x) = -1 for x < 0 and f(x) = 1 for x ≥ 0. It goes from -1 to 1 but never equals 0 — the jump at the origin skips it. The IVT's hypotheses are exactly what forbid that escape.
key_terms: Intermediate Value Theorem
Continuous f on [a, b] attains every value strictly between f(a) and f(b) at some c in (a, b)
Existence theorem
Guarantees something exists without locating it
Load-bearing hypothesis
Continuity on the closed interval — without it, values can be skipped
boxes: ap_alert

IVT, EVT, and MVT all require stating hypotheses for full FRQ credit. For IVT the sentence is: 'f is continuous on [a, b], and N is between f(a) and f(b), so by the IVT there exists c in (a, b) with f(c) = N.' Practice writing it verbatim.

sections.title: Root Hunting
sections.subtitle: Proving solutions exist
sections.body:
The IVT's killer app: proving an equation has a solution. To show f(x) = 0 has a root in (a, b), check that f is continuous on [a, b] and that f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs — then 0 lies between them, and the IVT delivers a c with f(c) = 0.

Example: show x^3 + x - 1 = 0 has a solution between 0 and 1. The function f(x) = x^3 + x - 1 is a polynomial, hence continuous everywhere — hypothesis verified in five words. f(0) = -1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0. Since f is continuous on [0, 1] and 0 is between -1 and 1, the IVT guarantees a c in (0, 1) with f(c) = 0. Three sentences, full credit, no solving required.

Equations that are not set to zero first: to show g(x) = 5 has a solution, either apply the IVT directly with N = 5, or define h(x) = g(x) - 5 and hunt a root of h. Both are accepted; the h-trick keeps every problem in the familiar sign-change format.

Bisection pushes the idea further: once a root is trapped in (0, 1), test the midpoint f(0.5) and keep the half with the sign change. Each test halves the interval — this is how calculators actually locate roots, and the exam occasionally asks which smaller interval must contain the root after evaluating a midpoint.
key_terms: Sign change
f(a) and f(b) with opposite signs puts 0 between them — the standard IVT setup for roots
Auxiliary function
Rewriting g(x) = N as h(x) = g(x) - N = 0 to convert any target value into a root hunt
Bisection
Repeatedly halving a sign-change interval to trap a root with increasing precision
boxes: ap_alert

The phrase 'must there exist' is IVT bait. 'Must f(c) = 4 for some c in (1, 3)?' — check continuity, check whether 4 is between f(1) and f(3), and answer with the theorem. If 4 is NOT between them, the answer is 'not guaranteed' — never 'no.'

sections.title: IVT from Tables
sections.subtitle: The exam's favorite delivery format
sections.body:
Table problems hand you selected values of a function announced to be continuous, then ask what the IVT forces. Suppose f is continuous with f(1) = 4, f(3) = -2, f(5) = 7. Between x = 1 and 3, every value in (-2, 4) is attained; between 3 and 5, everything in (-2, 7). So f(c) = 0 must happen at least twice — once in each interval, since 0 sits inside both brackets.

The word 'guarantee' is doing the work. The function might equal 0 ten more times — the table cannot rule behavior in or out between sample points. The IVT gives the floor: the minimum number of crossings consistent with the data. Counting that minimum (one crossing per tabulated sign change) is a recurring multiple-choice question.

What tables can NEVER prove: a maximum value, where the function is increasing, or that f stays between its tabulated values. Between samples, a continuous function can do anything continuous — spike to a million and return. Every guarantee must route through f's announced continuity plus an intermediate value argument; anything else is an unwarranted assumption about unseen behavior.

One nuance: IVT applies between each adjacent PAIR of table entries, because [1, 3] and [3, 5] are each closed intervals where the hypotheses hold. Chaining the conclusions interval by interval is the correct way to handle longer tables, and it is exactly how the multi-crossing count above worked.
key_terms: Guarantee
The minimum behavior the IVT forces from the data — a floor, not a census
Sign-change count
Each adjacent pair of opposite-sign table values forces at least one root in that subinterval
Unseen behavior
Whatever happens between sample points — unconstrained except by continuity
boxes: ap_alert

'Continuous' in the problem stem is not decoration — it is the hypothesis that activates the IVT, and quoting it is part of the answer. If a table problem does NOT announce continuity, the IVT guarantees nothing, and 'cannot be determined' becomes a serious candidate answer.

sections.title: What the IVT Does Not Say
sections.subtitle: Converse traps and boundary fine print
sections.body:
The IVT's converse is false, and the exam knows it. A function CAN hit every intermediate value while being discontinuous — pathologies like sin(1/x) extended through 0 hit every value in [-1, 1] on every neighborhood of 0, with no continuity. So 'f attains all intermediate values' does not certify continuity. Logic direction matters: continuity ⟹ intermediate values, never the reverse.

Strictness fine print: N must be strictly between f(a) and f(b). If f(a) = f(b), no N qualifies, and the IVT says precisely nothing (the function still might be constant or might swing wildly — no information). If the target equals an endpoint value, the theorem as stated does not apply, though the endpoint itself witnesses the value.

Uniqueness is never on offer. f(x) = sin(x) on [0, 5π] goes from 0 to 0 crossing height 1/2 five times. To get uniqueness you need IVT plus monotonicity — 'f is continuous and strictly increasing, so the root is unique' — a combination that becomes available with derivatives in Unit 5 and is a genuine FRQ pattern there.

Finally, the IVT needs BOTH hypotheses simultaneously: continuity AND a closed bracketed interval. Continuity on (a, b) with a limit blowing up at an endpoint, or continuity on a union of intervals dodging a discontinuity, voids the guarantee. When an exam answer choice says 'the IVT does not apply,' check the hypotheses — that choice is correct more often than students expect.
key_terms: False converse
Attaining intermediate values does not imply continuity
Strictly between
The IVT's N excludes the endpoint values f(a) and f(b)
IVT + monotonicity
The standard upgrade that converts 'at least one' into 'exactly one'
boxes: ap_alert

'At least one,' 'exactly one,' and 'at most one' are three different exam questions. IVT alone answers the first. The second needs IVT plus increasing/decreasing. The third needs monotonicity alone. Match the tool to the phrase before writing.

mcq.question: f is continuous on [2, 6] with f(2) = -3 and f(6) = 9. Which value must f attain on (2, 6)?
mcq.explanation: The IVT guarantees every value strictly between -3 and 9. Only 0 lies in that range; 10 and -5 are outside and not guaranteed.

mcq.question: g(x) = x^3 - 4x + 1. By the IVT, which interval(s) must contain a root of g?
mcq.explanation: g is continuous (polynomial). g(0) = 1, g(1) = -2, g(2) = 1: sign changes on (0, 1) AND on (1, 2), so the IVT forces a root inside each interval.

mcq.question: A continuous function h has values h(0) = 5, h(2) = -1, h(4) = 3, h(6) = -4. What is the minimum number of zeros h must have on (0, 6)?
mcq.explanation: Sign changes occur on (0,2), (2,4), and (4,6) — three changes, so at least three zeros. The actual count could be higher, but three is the guaranteed minimum.

mcq.question: f is continuous on [1, 5] with f(1) = 2 and f(5) = 2. Which statement must be true?

choices.C: f(x) = 0 has at most one solution in (1, 5)
choices.D: None of the above must be true

mcq.explanation: With f(1) = f(5) = 2, no value is strictly between the endpoint values, so the IVT guarantees nothing. The constant function f(x) = 2 defeats A and B, while a function dipping below zero and returning defeats C. None is forced.

mcq.question: Which hypothesis failure makes the IVT inapplicable to f(x) = 1/(x - 3) on [1, 5] for the target value 0?

choices.A: f(1) and f(5) are not of opposite sign
choices.C: 0 is not between f(1) and f(5)

mcq.explanation: f has an infinite discontinuity at x = 3 inside the interval, so the continuity hypothesis fails. (In fact f(1) = -1/2 and f(5) = 1/2 do bracket 0, yet f never equals 0 — showing exactly why the hypothesis matters.)

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5.
(a) Show that the equation f(x) = 0 has a solution in the interval (1, 2). State the theorem you use and verify its hypotheses.
(b) After computing f(1.5) = 2.875, state the smaller interval that must contain a root.
(c) Explain why the IVT cannot tell you the exact value of the root.
rubric: States f is a polynomial, hence continuous on [1, 2]
Computes f(1) = -2 < 0 and f(2) = 11 > 0 and notes 0 is between them; cites IVT for c in (1, 2)
Sign change now between f(1) < 0 and f(1.5) > 0: root in (1, 1.5)
Explains IVT is an existence theorem — it asserts a c exists but provides no construction
frq.model_answer: (a) f is a polynomial, so continuous everywhere, in particular on [1, 2]. f(1) = 1 + 2 - 5 = -2 and f(2) = 8 + 8 - 5 = 11. Since f is continuous on [1, 2] and 0 lies between -2 and 11, the IVT gives c in (1, 2) with f(c) = 0. (b) f(1) < 0 < f(1.5), so by the same argument the root lies in (1, 1.5). (c) The IVT only asserts existence: continuity forbids skipping values, but the theorem contains no mechanism for locating c — narrowing requires further evaluations, as in (b).

frq.question:
A continuous function g satisfies the table: g(0) = 8, g(1) = 3, g(2) = -2, g(3) = 0, g(4) = -5.
(a) What is the minimum number of solutions to g(x) = 1 on [0, 4]? Justify with the IVT.
(b) Must g attain the value 10 somewhere on [0, 4]? Explain.
(c) A student claims g is decreasing on [0, 2] because g(0) > g(1) > g(2). Explain the flaw.
rubric: Checks each adjacent pair and finds 1 is bracketed only by g(1) = 3 and g(2) = -2; concludes at least one solution, on (1, 2)
10 is not between any adjacent pair (max tabulated is 8), so not guaranteed — though possible
Notes the table only samples g; between samples g could rise and fall
Cites that decreasing-ness is a claim about all pairs of points, unverifiable from finitely many values
frq.model_answer: (a) On [1, 2], g goes from 3 to -2 and is continuous, with 1 strictly between; the IVT forces at least one c in (1, 2) with g(c) = 1. No other adjacent pair brackets 1, so the guaranteed minimum is 1. (b) No. The IVT only forces values between tabulated endpoints pairwise, and 10 exceeds every tabulated value. g might attain 10 between samples, but nothing requires it. (c) The table shows three decreasing sample values, but g is only sampled at integers — between them, a continuous g could oscillate up and down repeatedly. Monotonicity cannot be concluded from finitely many points.

frq.question:
Define f(x) = 1/x for x ≠ 0 with f(0) = 0, on the interval [-1, 1].
(a) Compute f(-1) and f(1), and note whether 1/2 lies between them.
(b) Determine whether f(c) = 1/2 has a solution in (-1, 1).
(c) Reconcile (a) and (b) with the IVT — why is there no contradiction?
rubric: f(-1) = -1, f(1) = 1, and 1/2 is strictly between them
Solves 1/x = 1/2 → x = 2, outside (-1, 1); checks f(0) = 0 ≠ 1/2: no solution in the interval
Identifies that f is discontinuous at 0 (infinite discontinuity)
Concludes the IVT's continuity hypothesis fails, so its conclusion is not guaranteed — no contradiction
frq.model_answer: (a) f(-1) = -1 and f(1) = 1; the value 1/2 is strictly between. (b) For x ≠ 0, f(x) = 1/2 forces x = 2, which is outside (-1, 1); and f(0) = 0. So f never equals 1/2 on (-1, 1). (c) The IVT requires continuity on the whole closed interval. f has an infinite discontinuity at 0 ∈ [-1, 1], so the theorem does not apply, and its conclusion may fail — exactly what happens. The example shows the continuity hypothesis is essential, not decorative.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Limits at Infinity and Asymptotic Behavior
hook: Zoom out far enough and every function shows its true character: some flatten toward a ceiling, some grow without bound, some keep oscillating forever. Limits at infinity are calculus's telescope — and they decide every horizontal asymptote you'll ever find.
learning_objectives: Evaluate limits as x → ∞ and x → -∞ for rational functions using dominant terms
Connect limits at infinity to horizontal asymptotes of graphs
Apply the three-case rule comparing degrees of numerator and denominator
Handle radical expressions at infinity, including the √(x^2) = |x| sign trap
Rank growth rates of logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential functions

sections.title: End Behavior as a Limit
sections.subtitle: What happens way out there
sections.body:
The notation lim x→∞ f(x) = L means: as x grows without bound, f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L and stays close. There is no point called infinity to plug in — the limit describes a trend. Likewise lim x→-∞ tracks behavior far to the left. These are called limits at infinity, distinct from the infinite limits of earlier chapters (which described unbounded OUTPUTS near a finite input).

The foundation stone: lim x→∞ 1/x = 0, and more generally 1/x^p → 0 for any p > 0. Dividing by something enormous yields something tiny. Every technique in this chapter is a scheme for rewriting functions so this one fact can finish the job.

When f(x) → L as x → ∞, the horizontal line y = L is a horizontal asymptote of the graph. Check both directions separately: a function has at most two horizontal asymptotes, one for each end. f(x) = arctan(x) genuinely has two — y = π/2 to the right, y = -π/2 to the left — and e^x has one (y = 0 leftward; rightward it grows without bound).

A limit at infinity can also be infinite — lim x→∞ x^2 = ∞ says the outputs outgrow every bound — or fail to exist entirely, as for sin(x), which oscillates forever without settling. Same trichotomy as always: settle, blow up, or wander.
key_terms: Limit at infinity
The value f(x) approaches as x → ∞ or x → -∞ — end behavior made precise
Horizontal asymptote
The line y = L when lim x→±∞ f(x) = L; at most one per direction
Reciprocal power fact
1/x^p → 0 as x → ∞ for every p > 0 — the engine behind all the algebra
boxes: ap_alert

Graphs may CROSS horizontal asymptotes — asymptotes describe end behavior, not forbidden territory. f(x) = sin(x)/x crosses y = 0 infinitely often. Only vertical asymptotes are uncrossable (a function value there doesn't exist).

sections.title: Rational Functions and the Degree Rule
sections.subtitle: Three cases that settle everything
sections.body:
For ratios of polynomials, end behavior is a contest between leading terms, and the contest has exactly three outcomes. Degrees equal: the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients. Denominator degree higher: the limit is 0. Numerator degree higher: the limit is ±∞ (sign determined by the leading terms; no horizontal asymptote).

Why it works: divide every term by the highest power of x in the denominator. In (3x^2 + 5x)/(2x^2 - 7), dividing by x^2 gives (3 + 5/x)/(2 - 7/x^2). Every fraction with x downstairs dies as x → ∞, leaving 3/2. Writing this division out is the rigorous version; reading off leading coefficients is the exam-speed version. Know both.

When the numerator wins, polynomial division reveals more structure: (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1 + 2/(x - 1), so the graph hugs the slant asymptote y = x + 1 at both ends. Slant (oblique) asymptotes occur exactly when the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's by one — a BC-flavored detail that strengthens curve analysis in Unit 5.

Dominance reasoning extends beyond polynomials: as x → ∞, the biggest power rules, so x^3 - 100x^2 → ∞ (the cube eventually crushes the huge-looking middle term). Internalize 'eventually' — end behavior is about the long run, and coefficients only matter within the same degree.
key_terms: Degree rule
Equal degrees: ratio of leading coefficients. Bottom-heavy: 0. Top-heavy: ±∞
Dominant term
The highest-degree term, which controls a polynomial's end behavior outright
Slant asymptote
The line a top-heavy-by-one rational function approaches, found by polynomial division
boxes: ap_alert

Check x → ∞ and x → -∞ separately when the answer is ±∞: (x^3)/(x^2 + 1) → ∞ rightward but -∞ leftward. Multiple-choice traps routinely offer the right magnitude with the wrong sign for the leftward limit.

sections.title: Radicals at Infinity
sections.subtitle: The |x| trap
sections.body:
